canonical_statement: The Standards chapter presents current ADA clinical practice recommendations; the detailed evidence-grading system and guideline-development methodology are delegated to the separate Introduction and Methodology.
CKD is diagnosed by persistent albuminuria, eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², or other manifestations of kidney damage.
CKD attributed to diabetes occurs in approximately 20–40% of people with diabetes.
CKD in type 1 diabetes typically develops after about 10 years, whereas CKD may be present at the time type 2 diabetes is diagnosed.

For albuminuria assessment, a spot UACR is preferred in most clinical settings; because biological variability is high, two of three UACR specimens collected within 3–6 months should be abnormal before classifying moderately or severely elevated albuminuria.
Combining creatinine and cystatin C filtration markers is more accurate than either marker alone and can support better clinical decisions.

The typical clinical presentation of CKD in diabetes includes long diabetes duration, retinopathy, albuminuria without gross hematuria, and gradually progressive eGFR loss, but atypical presentations occur.
Table 11.1 identifies Type 1 diabetes duration under 5 years or no retinopathy as a reason to consider nondiabetic kidney disease in a person with CKD and diabetes.
Table 11.1 identifies Active urine sediment, such as red blood cells or cellular casts as a reason to consider nondiabetic kidney disease in a person with CKD and diabetes.
Table 11.1 identifies Chronically well-managed blood glucose as a reason to consider nondiabetic kidney disease in a person with CKD and diabetes.
Table 11.1 identifies Rapidly declining eGFR as a reason to consider nondiabetic kidney disease in a person with CKD and diabetes.

Table 11.1 identifies Rapidly increasing or very high UACR above 300 mg/g or urine protein/creatinine above 500 mg/g as a reason to consider nondiabetic kidney disease in a person with CKD and diabetes.
CKD staging integrates both eGFR category and albuminuria category because albuminuria at any eGFR is associated with cardiovascular disease, CKD progression, and mortality.
Stage G5 is kidney failure; G1 and G2 require evidence of kidney damage such as increased albuminuria rather than eGFR alone.
Figure 11.1 classifies albuminuria as A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30–299 mg/g, and A3 at least 300 mg/g, and GFR as G1 at least 90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, and G5 below 15 mL/min/1.73 m².

Figure 11.1 links higher GFR/albuminuria risk categories to more frequent monitoring and nephrology referral, ranging from annual screening in low-risk cells to treatment/referral four or more times per year in the highest-risk cells.
AKI is a rapid decline in kidney function over hours to days, characterized by increased serum creatinine and/or decreased urine output.
The chapter reports that adults with diabetes have fivefold higher hospitalization rates for dialysis-requiring AKI than adults without diabetes (risk ratio 5.0, 95% CI 4.8–5.1).
Randomized trials cited by the chapter did not show increased AKI risk from SGLT2 inhibitors in advanced kidney disease or in people at high cardiovascular risk with normal kidney function.
Serum creatinine increases up to 30% from baseline during RAS blockade should not be confused with AKI in the absence of volume depletion.
Both albuminuria and eGFR should be monitored at least annually to detect CKD progression, superimposed kidney disease, medication effects, and need for nephrology referral.
When eGFR is below 60 mL/min/1.73 m², medication dosing should be verified, nephrotoxin exposure minimized, and CKD complications assessed.
Table 11.2 pairs Blood pressure >130/80 mmHg with evaluation using blood pressure, weight, and BMI.
Table 11.2 pairs Volume overload with evaluation using history, physical examination, and weight.
Table 11.2 pairs Electrolyte abnormalities with evaluation using serum electrolytes.
Table 11.2 pairs Metabolic acidosis with evaluation using serum electrolytes.
Table 11.2 pairs Anemia with evaluation using hemoglobin, iron, iron saturation, and ferritin testing if indicated.
Table 11.2 pairs Metabolic bone disease with evaluation using serum calcium, phosphate, PTH, and vitamin 25(OH)D.

Table 11.2 notes that CKD complications generally become prevalent below eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and laboratory evaluation is generally every 6–12 months in G3, every 3–5 months in G4, and every 1–3 months in G5, adjusted for symptoms or therapy changes.

Table 11.3 lists blood glucose management, blood pressure management, ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy, smoking cessation, weight loss, dietary change, physical activity, and SGLT2 inhibitor/MRA/GLP-1 RA therapy as interventions that lower albuminuria.

The chapter states that the proven primary prevention measures for CKD in diabetes are blood glucose management and blood pressure management; routine RAS inhibition solely to prevent CKD is not supported in the absence of hypertension or albuminuria.

In GRADE, 5,047 participants with type 2 diabetes on metformin were followed for about 5 years, and liraglutide, sitagliptin, glimepiride, and insulin glargine did not differ in kidney-protective effects for CKD prevention; SGLT2 inhibitors were not included.

For nondialysis CKD, protein intake above 20% of daily calories or above 1.3 g/kg/day has been associated with increased albuminuria, faster kidney function loss, and cardiovascular mortality and should be avoided.
Dietary sodium restriction below 2,300 mg/day may help manage blood pressure and reduce cardiovascular risk; sodium and potassium targets should be individualized.
Intensive glucose lowering delays onset and progression of albuminuria, but eGFR benefits may take at least 2 years in type 2 diabetes and more than 10 years in type 1 diabetes to manifest.
In CKD, intensive glucose lowering carries greater hypoglycemia and mortality risk in some populations; less intensive A1C goals may therefore be appropriate in people with substantial comorbidity.
A1C becomes less reliable in advanced CKD; glycated albumin and fructosamine, reflecting approximately 15–30 days of glycemia, can assist clinical management.
Blood pressure variability is more frequent and larger in CKD, and the chapter reports a 47% greater risk of kidney failure per 10-mmHg increase in variability (HR 1.47, 95% CI 1.09–1.99).
In BPROAD, intensive systolic blood pressure treatment was associated with lower incident albuminuria than standard treatment (11.29 vs 13.84 events per 100 person-years; HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77–0.97).

population.label: 12,821 people with diabetes and elevated cardiovascular risk

canonical_statement: For UACR 30–299 mg/g, maximally tolerated ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy reduces progression to more advanced albuminuria, slows CKD progression, and reduces cardiovascular events, but trials have not shown reduced progression to kidney failure.

Long-term double-blind studies cited by the chapter did not show kidney-protective effects from ACE inhibitors or ARBs in normotensive people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes in the primary-prevention setting.
Among people with diabetes and/or CKD receiving ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy, SGLT2 inhibitor initiation was associated with lower hyperkalemia risk (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.96).

population.label: Individuals with diabetes and/or CKD receiving ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy

canonical_statement: SGLT2 inhibitors reduce tubular glucose reabsorption, weight, systemic and intraglomerular pressure, and albuminuria, and slow GFR loss through mechanisms that appear partly independent of glycemia.
The chapter states that GLP-1 receptor agonists improve kidney outcomes, with proposed nonmetabolic mechanisms including anti-inflammatory, antioxidative, and immunomodulatory actions.
Figure 11.2 places healthy eating, physical activity, smoking cessation, weight management, and regular risk-factor reassessment every 3–6 months at the base of CKD management.
Figure 11.2 places maximally tolerated RAS inhibition as foundational therapy when albuminuria and/or hypertension is present.

Figure 11.2 positions SGLT2 inhibition for type 2 diabetes at eGFR at least 20 mL/min/1.73 m² with continuation until dialysis or transplant, and GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy as a complementary first-line cardiorenal option with demonstrated benefit.

Figure 11.2 identifies a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker and/or diuretic as blood-pressure therapy when needed to achieve the individualized goal, and moderate- or high-intensity statin therapy as standard risk reduction.

Figure 11.2 lists additional risk-based therapy including other glucose-lowering drugs, nonsteroidal MRA therapy, steroidal MRA for resistant hypertension when appropriate, antiplatelet therapy for clinical ASCVD, and additional lipid-lowering therapy based on ASCVD risk and lipids.
Figure 11.2 notes that finerenone is currently the only nonsteroidal MRA with proven clinical kidney and cardiovascular benefits.

The chapter summarizes cardiovascular outcome trials in which empagliflozin, canagliflozin, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and semaglutide reduced secondary kidney outcomes; these analyses were limited because the study populations were not selected primarily for CKD and kidney effects were secondary outcomes.

CREDENCE randomized 4,401 adults with type 2 diabetes, UACR 300–5,000 mg/g, and eGFR 30–90 mL/min/1.73 m²; canagliflozin reduced kidney failure by 32% and the primary cardiorenal composite by 30% on background ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy in more than 99% of participants.
In DAPA-CKD, dapagliflozin reduced the primary composite of sustained eGFR decline, kidney failure, cardiovascular death, or kidney death (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.51–0.72; P<0.001).

population.label: 4,304 participants with CKD; 67.5% had type 2 diabetes

canonical_statement: In DAPA-CKD, dapagliflozin reduced the kidney composite of sustained eGFR decline of at least 50%, kidney failure, or kidney death (HR 0.56, 95% CI 0.45–0.68; P<0.001).

population.label: 4,304 participants with CKD; 67.5% had type 2 diabetes

canonical_statement: In DAPA-CKD, dapagliflozin reduced cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.55–0.92; P=0.009).

population.label: 4,304 participants with CKD; 67.5% had type 2 diabetes

canonical_statement: In EMPA-KIDNEY, empagliflozin lowered the risk of kidney disease progression or cardiovascular death (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.64–0.82; P<0.001).

population.label: 6,609 participants with kidney disease; approximately half had diabetes

concept.text: Kidney disease progression or cardiovascular death

canonical_statement: The chapter emphasizes that SGLT2 inhibitor kidney and cardiovascular benefits persist at eGFR as low as 20 mL/min/1.73 m² even when glucose lowering is blunted, supporting initiation at the eGFR 20 threshold.

FLOW enrolled 3,533 participants with type 2 diabetes and CKD and reported a 24% lower hazard of the major kidney disease composite with semaglutide versus placebo; kidney-specific events excluding cardiovascular death were 21% lower.

The chapter notes uncertainty about whether semaglutide’s kidney benefit in FLOW reflects a unique kidney-protective effect versus its combined effects on A1C, blood pressure, weight, and cardiovascular outcomes.

No published randomized kidney-outcomes trial of tirzepatide is cited; SURMOUNT-2 showed lower albuminuria, but only 5% of participants had eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and 31% had albuminuria at baseline.
Most GLP-1 receptor agonists can be used at low eGFR for cardiovascular protection, but lixisenatide and exenatide depend on kidney elimination and have limited data in severe kidney impairment.
FIDELIO-DKD reported a lower primary kidney composite with finerenone than placebo (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.73–0.93; P=0.001).

population.label: 5,734 people with CKD and type 2 diabetes

concept.text: Kidney failure, sustained eGFR decrease >40%, or kidney death

canonical_statement: FIDELIO-DKD reported a lower key cardiovascular composite with finerenone than placebo (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75–0.99; P=0.03).

FIGARO-DKD reported a lower primary cardiovascular composite with finerenone versus placebo (12.4% vs 14.2%; HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.76–0.98; P=0.03).

canonical_statement: In FIGARO-DKD, hyperkalemia occurred in 10.8% of finerenone recipients versus 5.3% of placebo recipients, and 1.2% of finerenone recipients stopped treatment because of hyperkalemia.
FIDELITY pooled 13,171 participants and reported a lower cardiovascular composite with finerenone versus placebo (12.7% vs 14.4%; HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.95; P=0.002).

concept.text: Sustained ≥57% eGFR decrease or kidney death

canonical_statement: All recent kidney and cardiovascular outcome trials discussed for diabetes and CKD were conducted on background maximally tolerated RAS blockade, supporting optimization of ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy before or alongside combination cardiorenal therapy.

A population-based cohort cited by the chapter associated combined GLP-1 RA and SGLT2 inhibitor treatment with 30% lower major adverse cardiovascular event risk and 57% lower serious kidney event risk versus GLP-1 RA alone; adding SGLT2 inhibition to GLP-1 RA was associated with 29% lower major adverse cardiovascular event risk versus SGLT2 inhibitor alone.

CONFIDENCE randomized participants with type 2 diabetes, CKD, eGFR above 30 and below 90 mL/min/1.73 m², and UACR above 100 and below 5,000 mg/g to finerenone, empagliflozin, or both; simultaneous initiation reduced UACR 52% at 180 days, 32% more than empagliflozin alone and 29% more than finerenone alone.

The evidence supporting simultaneous finerenone plus SGLT2 inhibitor initiation in the chapter is centered on the albuminuria surrogate from CONFIDENCE rather than a completed hard kidney-outcome comparison.
During pregnancy, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct renin inhibitors, MRAs, SGLT2 inhibitors, and neprilysin inhibitors are contraindicated because of potential fetal harm.

The chapter identifies methyldopa, labetalol, and long-acting nifedipine as effective and safe antihypertensive options in pregnancy, with hydralazine considered for acute severe hypertension or preeclampsia.
A post hoc DAPA-CKD analysis cited by the chapter found dapagliflozin effects in stage G4 CKD with albuminuria consistent with the overall trial and no evidence of increased risk.

The chapter states that more evidence is needed on SGLT2 inhibitor safety and efficacy in kidney failure; the Renal Lifecycle trial is ongoing in individuals with eGFR at or below 25 mL/min/1.73 m² or kidney failure.
A 12-week prospective open-label study of 13 dialysis patients denied transplant because of high BMI reported mean weight loss of 4.6 ± 2.4 kg with semaglutide.
In a national cohort of 151,649 people with type 2 diabetes initiating dialysis, GLP-1–based therapy was associated with 23% lower mortality and a 66% higher chance of transplant waitlisting.
An observational study cited by the chapter associated GLP-1–based therapy at dialysis initiation with lower major adverse cardiovascular event risk (adjusted HR 0.65; P<0.001).

population.label: People with diabetes at dialysis initiation

canonical_statement: The same observational dialysis study associated GLP-1–based therapy with lower all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.63; P<0.001) during median 1.4-year follow-up.

population.label: People with diabetes at dialysis initiation

canonical_statement: The chapter cautions that the observational dialysis GLP-1 study had methodological limitations, including likely inclusion of people with acute kidney injury.

Nephrology referral should also be considered for continuously rising UACR, continuously declining eGFR, uncertain etiology, difficult management problems such as anemia or resistant hypertension, and advanced CKD requiring kidney-replacement planning.
The chapter reports that nephrology consultation at stage G4 CKD has been associated with reduced cost, improved quality of care, and delayed need for dialysis.
